headline: The Satellite That Sees War: Fascinating Methodology, Sixteen Trades, and the Silence of the Unwitnessed Losses
lede: A trading system that watches conflict zones from orbit using free NASA fire-detection data is a genuinely interesting idea — and the methodology has real precedent in open-source intelligence. What the numbers do not yet warrant is the conclusion drawn from them.
body:
The appeal of the setup is hard to dismiss entirely. NASA's Fire Information for Resource Management System — FIRMS, a free public platform distributing near-real-time thermal-anomaly data from the VIIRS instrument aboard the Suomi-NPP and NOAA-20 satellites — has been used with measurable success by open-source investigators to track active fighting since at least 2022. Bellingcat and independent researchers have cross-referenced FIRMS fire counts against confirmed artillery strikes in Ukraine, finding that large-scale bombardment campaigns do register as statistically anomalous clusters of thermal hotspots. The October 7 Gaza spike described in the post — a claimed jump from a baseline of six fires per day to sixty-nine — is, in principle, exactly the kind of macro signal the system was built to surface. Whether those specific numbers match the archived FIRMS record is unverified here, but the direction of the claim is plausible: FIRMS detects fires down to roughly fifty square meters under optimal conditions, and an attack of that scale would have produced thermal signatures visible from the 375-meter VIIRS pixel grid.

The Kursk observation is similarly coherent. Researchers examining the Russia-Ukraine conflict from August 2024 noted that fighting in Kursk Oblast was captured on the NASA fire map within hours of the Ukrainian cross-border offensive, with heat-sensor data logging unusual signatures across an area of approximately 1,500 square kilometers. Charter'97 and other monitoring outlets were already citing FIRMS data within days of the incursion. Whether a private anomaly detector would have caught the buildup four days prior — the post's most precise claim — depends on exactly how baseline was calculated and what threshold triggered an alert; the methodology is not disclosed in enough detail to reproduce or audit.

The Syria signal, on the other hand, deserves more caution. The offensive that ultimately brought down Bashar al-Assad's government began on 27 November 2024 when Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham — the Islamist coalition led by HTS — launched its advance from Idlib. A thermal alert on 16 November would have preceded the kinetic opening by eleven days; but the Assad government's eventual collapse on 8 December owed as much to the near-total collapse of Russian air cover (Moscow had redeployed most of its Syrian garrison to Ukraine), the disintegration of Syrian Army morale, and a loss of Iranian ground support as it did to any detectable fire signature. The FIRMS data may well have shown unusual pre-offensive activity; the causal chain from that data to a regime-change trade, however, is considerably longer and more contingent than the post implies.

The financial claim is where skepticism becomes obligatory. Sixteen trades over 270 days is not a trading strategy — it is an anecdote. Financial statisticians generally require hundreds of independent trades before distinguishing skill from noise with any confidence, and even then demand controls for look-ahead bias, transaction costs, and the particular luck of the entry and exit timing. The reported result of $500 growing to $7,778 — a 15.5-fold gain — implies highly concentrated, asymmetric sizing on convex instruments: Polymarket outcome contracts (a prediction market where shares pay $1 at resolution and $0 otherwise), gold, VIX-linked products, or cryptocurrency derivatives as the screenshot's integration list suggests. Convex bets constructed around rare, high-magnitude events can produce extraordinary returns in a short window. They can also go to zero. The post acknowledges five losses but does not disclose their magnitude relative to the wins, which is precisely the parameter that determines whether a strategy has positive expected value or is simply fortunate exposure to a fat-tailed outcome.

There is also a structural problem that no filter rule can fully resolve: the moment a FIRMS anomaly becomes widely known — cited by wire services, incorporated into Polymarket prices, reflected in gold and VIX — any informational edge it once offered has already decayed. The post's own admission that the bot "kept buying Kursk after the anomaly became the new normal" is a precise description of alpha decay, the phenomenon by which a once-profitable signal loses predictive power as markets learn to price it. The proposed fix — skipping any signal where the seven-day baseline has itself tripled — is a reasonable heuristic, but it is calibrated on three events. A heuristic calibrated on three events that successfully explains three outcomes is not a rule; it is a post-hoc description of those three outcomes. Real systematic trading requires out-of-sample validation: applying the ruleset to events the bot did not see during development, measuring performance, and only then making claims about forward-looking edge.

None of this renders the underlying idea worthless. Satellite-derived thermal data is genuinely underused as a geopolitical input; hedge funds and commodity desks already pay for commercial satellite imagery and alternative-data feeds that cost vastly more than FIRMS' zero-dollar price tag, precisely because pre-news signals have real value. The post's core intuition — that physical evidence from space sometimes precedes media coverage of conflict events — has scholarly and practical support. What it lacks is the one thing no amount of clever engineering can substitute for: a statistically adequate sample of out-of-sample results. Eleven wins from sixteen trades is interesting. It will become meaningful somewhere around the hundred-and-sixteenth.

concepts.definition: Fire Information for Resource Management System — a free NASA platform that distributes near-real-time thermal-anomaly and active-fire data globally, refreshed roughly every three to six hours, drawn from the MODIS and VIIRS satellite instruments aboard several Earth-observation satellites. Originally designed to track wildfires, it has been applied to conflict monitoring because large-scale bombardment and destruction generate thermal signatures detectable from orbit.

Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite — a multispectral sensor aboard the Suomi-NPP and NOAA-20/21 satellites that detects mid-infrared radiation emitted by fires and other heat sources at a spatial resolution of 375 meters per pixel. VIIRS data forms the backbone of NASA FIRMS and is significantly more sensitive at night and for small fires than its predecessor, MODIS.

A peer-to-peer prediction market — now regulated by the CFTC following a 2025 exchange acquisition — where participants buy and sell binary contracts on real-world outcomes (elections, geopolitical events, economic data) priced between zero and one dollar, paying out $1 if the event occurs and $0 if it does not. Prices aggregate crowd probability estimates in real time, making Polymarket a source of implied odds for trading around geopolitical events.

The erosion of a signal's predictive edge as markets become aware of and begin pricing the same information. In geopolitical trading, alpha decay occurs when a previously obscure satellite data feed or anomaly indicator becomes cited in news coverage, at which point the market has already moved to incorporate its signal, eliminating any profit opportunity for latecomers. The post's 'new normal' filter is a practical response to one form of alpha decay.

A wager or trade whose payoff is disproportionately large relative to the stake — typically a binary outcome contract or deep-out-of-the-money option that pays a multiple of the investment if correct. Convex bets can produce dramatic gains from a small number of winners even when most individual trades lose, which makes them prone to producing misleadingly impressive track records over short windows.

The practice of testing a trading rule or predictive model on data it was not used to construct — events that occurred after the strategy was designed — to distinguish genuine predictive power from retrospective curve-fitting. A strategy back-tested only on the same events that inspired its construction has not been out-of-sample validated and cannot reliably claim forward-looking edge.

fact_check: The post's three headline examples (Gaza October 7, Kursk August 2024, Syria November 2024) are broadly consistent with documented FIRMS usage in conflict monitoring, but the specific fire-count figures and lead times are unverified against the archived FIRMS record. The financial claim rests on sixteen trades — far too small a sample to assess statistical significance. The 15.5x return figure ($500 to $7,778) implies aggressive position sizing on convex instruments; no information is given on loss magnitude relative to wins, making expected-value estimation impossible. The 'four days' Kursk lead-time and 'three weeks' Syria lead-time are unverifiable without access to the bot's specific baseline parameters and signal thresholds.
